permissionProbe.contract: the real on-disk permissions are the whole boundary; the Agent never chmods or chowns user data; fixtures prepare only their own trees

rootClaim.implementation: WorkspacePin.capture on Linux takes an exclusive claim file under /tmp/dsh-agent-root-locks keyed by the directory dev:ino (aliases converge on the same claim), with the controller-lock PID-liveness and fstat-vs-lstat identity discipline for reclaiming a verifiably dead owner's claim; nested captures in one process refcount (the container shell re-pin does not self-deadlock); an unavailable lock directory degrades to the previous single-database semantics with an observable marker instead of breaking a working workspace
rootClaim.publicContract: a conflicting claim surfaces as the existing WORKSPACE_BUSY; the per-dataDir journal, stop evidence and release semantics are unchanged

platforms.rootRegression: 1821 tests, 1763 pass, 0 fail, 58 skipped, exit 0 (log: tmp/integration/workspace-permissions-root-regression.log); the suite is registered in npm test and Windows/Ubuntu CI

observed: A second Agent process with a different dataDir is refused WORKSPACE_BUSY on the same physical root while a live holder keeps the claim, and a SIGKILLed holder's claim is reclaimed on the next admission; the refusal came from the claim, not from a journal row.
An alias of the held root converges on the same claim; nested same-process captures never self-deadlock; a fully released claim lets an independent process pin the root again.

The real-Docker probe shows the permission boundary end to end: operator-granted access works, owner-private files and subtrees fail closed with EACCES, chmod/chown by the capability-less worker answer EPERM, and worker-created files carry uid 65532.
limitations: Group-based operator grants (chgrp 65532) need a root-prepared fixture and are not verified here; world-access is the verified grant shape.

The claim directory is per-boot /tmp: crash-stale claims for never-revisited inodes accumulate until reboot; PID reuse after a holder's death is not distinguished (same trade-off as the controller lock).

A different service user owning the lock directory degrades to single-database semantics (observable via the rootLockDegrades marker) rather than coordinating across users; cross-user coordination is open.
Windows keeps path-based admission only; no directory claim is claimed there. Account/AppContainer/network/filesystem isolation is still not claimed anywhere.
